question: How many millions of individual income tax returns will claim the refundable child tax credit or additional child tax credit for tax year 2027, as first published by the IRS Statistics of Income Division in Publication 1304, Table 3.3, all returns total row, conditional on no legislation enacted by December 31, 2027 changing the $2,500 earned-income threshold operative under IRC §24(h)(6)?
resolutionSource: IRS Statistics of Income, Individual Income Tax Returns Complete Report (Publication 1304), Table 3.3, all returns total row, refundable child tax credit or additional child tax credit, number of returns. Multiply the published return count by 0.000001 and round to the published forecast precision. Resolve from the first IRS publication for tax year 2027; later corrections or revisions do not apply.
conditional_on: No legislation enacted by 2027-12-31 changes the IRC §24(d)(1)(B)(i) earned-income threshold of $2,500 for tax year 2027; current law holds. The $2,500 operative amount is applied by IRC §24(h)(6), while §24(d)(1)(B)(i) contains the underlying $3,000 amount.

reasoning.content: Tax year 2027 Additional Child Tax Credit total claims under current law

Framing: Resolve the first IRS SOI Publication 1304 Table 3.3 estimate for the number of all individual returns claiming the refundable child tax credit or additional child tax credit for tax year 2027. The unit is millions of returns. The forecast is conditional on the $2,500 earned-income threshold remaining operative through December 31, 2027. The registered resolutionDate is December 31, 2029, representing the end of the ledger's official first-release window rather than a specific scheduled publication day.

reasoning.name: Current-law verification

reasoning.content: Base rate: Comparable current-law observations 2018, 2019, 2020, 2022, and 2023 are 20.450, 19.868, 19.119, 18.077, and 17.626 million. Mean = 19.028 million, sample standard deviation = 1.184 million, and range = 17.626–20.450 million. Annualized declines are -0.583, -0.748, -0.521, and -0.451 million, averaging -0.576 million per year. The 2021 temporary-law value is excluded.

Benchmarks: Last-print persistence gives 17.6 million. A linear current-law trend gives 15.3 million for 2027. Sparse expanding-window checks produce approximate MAE of 0.594 million for persistence and 0.217 million for the trend, so the trend is selected while its interval is deliberately widened.

OLS on (year, millions) = {(2018,20.450468),(2019,19.867646),(2020,19.119249),(2022,18.077),(2023,17.626084)} gives slope -0.569 million/year and 2027 point 15.27, rounded to 15.3. Historical comparable-level sigma = 1.184. Four-year/policy/sampling widening factor = 1.25. Central 80% p10–p90 half-width = 1.28 × 1.184 × 1.25 = 1.89; bounds = 15.3 ± 1.9 = 13.4–17.2 million. The corresponding central 90% half-width is 1.645 × 1.184 × 1.25 = 2.43, giving 12.8–17.7 million.

Prior/update/interval: Prior = 17.6 million last-print persistence using the 2023 IRS proxy observation. Selected model = current-law linear trend over five comparable 2018–2023 prints, which moves the point -2.3 million from persistence because the declining pattern is repeated and outperforms persistence in sparse walk-forward checks. Policy update = 0.0 million because current law already permanently retains the $2,500 threshold. Interval method = central p10–p90 interval from empirical comparable-level dispersion widened 1.25 for the four-year horizon, statutory-condition risk, sample estimation, and filing behavior; implied 80% bounds are 13.4–17.2 million.

Counter-consideration: The trend sample is short, skips 2021 because of temporary law, and could overstate decline if the 2022–2023 reduction reflects transitory filing behavior. A stable qualifying-child population, stronger low-income employment, or more taxpayers exhausting the nonrefundable credit could keep claims near the 17.6 million persistence benchmark.

Tail stress: Above 17.2 million would require a material reversal, such as unexpectedly strong growth in eligible low- and middle-income families, a shift from nonrefundable CTC to ACTC caused by lower tax liabilities, or administrative changes increasing claims without changing the statutory threshold. Below 13.4 million would require a substantially faster decline in qualifying-child returns, employment or earnings patterns moving families outside the refundable formula, stricter identification enforcement, or a large change in filing behavior.

Review disposition: Accepted the clarifications that the 2023 Publication 4801 value is a historical proxy and that the 80% interval is central p10–p90. Forecast: 15.3 million returns, with an 80% interval of 13.4 to 17.2 million.
